doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Bringing Jaco Pastorius into Rawls's band
summary: He hired Jaco, who met Don Alias and Bobby Colomby, leading to his first album; Jaco's sad decline.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Well speaking of bass players, with Jaco Pastorius, was that your choice to have him come?

Absolutely. Jaco’s story is really sad to me. Because he was an incredible musician. There’s absolutely no doubt about that. And we used to work here, the Bachelor’s Three, there were three places, Cohen’s by Joe Namath and some other people, and the one in Fort Lauderdale where Jaco was a house musician in Peter Graves’ band. And we played there quite a bit, I don’t know, two or three times a year, whatever. And there was Jaco playing. He was just a great bass player. Everybody knew that. So this was at the same time when our bass player was going to leave after the Denver incident and we needed a bass player. So I got the bright idea to say I wonder if this guy would be interested in joining Lou’s band, although the kind of stuff that Lou was doing was not where Jaco wanted to be, I was confident that he could do that with one hand tied behind his back and what would be the problem. So anyway I offered him the gig and he said yes I’d like to do that. So anyway, the bottom line is it really wasn’t what he wanted to play, but he © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -14-

did manage to hook up with a percussionist, Don Alias, who had lots of good connections in the jazz industry as well as the basic music industry, and he got him together with Bobby Colomby, the producer for Blood, Sweat and Tears, and so that’s how the first Jaco album actually came to be. So in a way I kind of pat myself on the back by saying hey, I mean Don Alias was on my gig and they knew each other, but once they were in the same band things get tighter. And so as a result of that, I think Jaco’s story kind of took on its perspective. What’s sad about it is when I met Jaco he was all into running barefoot on the beach and drinking orange juice and he was a health nut and all of that. And as time went on the psychosis that he had, which is well documented now, became more and more obvious and he really had mental problems and then couple that with drug abuse and eventually he met his unfortunate demise that way, and that’s sad. But I do feel I had a little something to do with his getting where it was. It would have happened anyway, I firmly believe that somebody with that kind of immense talent and something to say, you know, it would have happened. It just happened to happen that way.
